The Motherload is the source location of a gold deposit. This is the result of molten geological activity deep in the Earth. When water passes over a motherload it wears away the gold and carries it downstream. When gold is found in a location like in a creek bed, people will try to follow that trail back upstream in search of the motherload.

This process is complicated by the fact that rivers move over time, not just down, but sideways too. If the gold found in a creek is on top of the creek bed, then it is likely the water is still in contact with the motherload, and your odds of finding it are improved.

If the gold is found deep in the creek bed, or away from the water's current location (say 50 feet up the side of a river bank, and no lower. Then your odds of finding the motherload are greatly diminished as the river upstream has long since moved away from it. You can follow the gold upstream until it stops, and see if it leaves the stream, continuing upward on land. If not, then start searching sideways, on either side, because the motherload is likely nearby, if it still exists at all.

Geologists will also do this using core sampling, to create a map of a gold bearing region, in an attempt to follow the direction of the gold, and it's eventual source. Based on the sampling results, a region that is bearing gold in the samples can be not only mapped, but an economic potential value for that land is thus created. Geologists can also use core sampling to map deposits that exist very deep underground. If the percentage of gold found is high enough, then there is often still a profitable venture to be had by mining it. It's a cost benefit analysis. There are all kinds of untouched known and owned deposits of gold that go unharvested because the current gold price remains too low to justify the further needed investment.

On a side note, tampering with the samples, say by adding extra gold flakes to enhance the sample quality of the core samples, is not unheard of in the gold industry.
